hook_text: Ten rolls, no six. The next roll has to be a six, right? The die disagrees.
clip_script: A fair die has six equal faces, so the chance of a six is 1 out of 6. Roll it 120 times and a sixth of 120 is 20, so expect about 20 sixes. About. Not exactly. One class rolled 60 times and got 8 ones, 11 twos, 9 threes, 12 fours, 10 fives and 10 sixes. Uneven? Perfectly normal. Now the trap. You roll ten times and no six appears. Is a six due? No. The die has no memory. The eleventh roll is still 1 out of 6, exactly like the first. The early shortage is never paid back; it just gets diluted as the rolls pile up, which is why, over thousands of rolls, the fraction of sixes creeps towards one sixth. Chance times tries gives the prediction. The word about keeps it honest.
visual_style: A die tumbles across a whiteboard; a tally table fills in for 60 rolls; ten rolls with no six flash red; a speech bubble saying six is due gets crossed out; a line graph of the fraction of sixes settles towards one sixth.
pacing: Brisk setup, a pause on the ten-roll drought, a firm no, a slow finish on the settling graph.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson to calculate probabilities, tally relative frequencies and predict results with chance times tries.
